papers.title: Working memory and reasoning benefit from different modes of large-scale brain dynamics in healthy older adults
papers.abstract: Abstract Researchers have proposed that solving complex reasoning problems, a key indicator of fluid intelligence, involves the same cognitive processes as solving working memory tasks. This proposal is supported by an overlap of the functional brain activations associated with the two types of tasks and by high correlations between inter-individual differences in performance. We replicated these findings in fifty-three older subjects but also showed that solving reasoning and working memory problems benefits from different configurations of the functional connectome and that this dissimilarity increases with higher difficulty load. Specifically, superior performance in a typical working memory paradigm (n-back) was associated with up-regulation of modularity (increased between-network segregation), whereas performance in the reasoning task was associated with effective down-regulation of modularity. We also showed that working memory training promotes task-invariant increases in modularity. Since superior reasoning performance is associated with down-regulation of modular dynamics, training may thus have fostered an inefficient way of solving the reasoning tasks. This could help explain why working memory training does little to promote complex reasoning performance. The study concludes that complex reasoning abilities cannot be reduced to working memory and suggests the need to reconsider the feasibility of using working memory training interventions to attempt to achieve effects that transfer to broader cognition.

papers.title: Representation and strategy in reasoning : an individual differences approach
papers.abstract: Individual differences in reasoning have been observed in a wide variety of tasks.Descriptions of the variation in response have been framed in terms of use of different strategies that invoke different representations.This thesis argues that in order to convert descriptions into explanations of performance it is necessary to compare and combine psychometric accounts with computational accounts of the processes underlying representation selection and use.Descriptions of strategies, representations and algorithms and their inter-relationships are necessary for a full account of reasoning behaviour.Two large-scale studies of deductive reasoning are presented to illustrate this approach in action, and the inadequacy of accounts that do not provide accounts at all these levels.The first compares two theoretically motivated methods for solving categorial syllogisms, the second study assesses learning from and learning within a multimodal logic course called Hyperproof.These studies are compared to measures of spatial ability, field-independence/dependence, and serialist/holist learning style.The interaction of students' styles of learning with different presentations of information generalises across the domains.This generality is best expressed when psychometric and computational accounts of reasoning are consolidated.Many thanks to my supervisors Keith Sterining and Jon Oberlander whose complementary styles and enthusiasms maintained my own.Keith's comment that "it only takes one zebra to make a species" has stayed with me, summing up the comfort and inspiration his supervision has had.Also thanks to Richard Cox, John Lee and the

papers.title: The Cognitive Underpinnings of Multiply-Constrained Problem Solving
papers.abstract: An individual encounters problem of varying difficulty every day. Each problem may include a different number of constraints. Multiply-constrained problems, such as the compound remote associates, are commonly used to study problem solving. Since their development, multiply-constrained problems have been related to creativity and insight. Moreover, research has investigated the cognitive abilities underlying problem solving abilities. In the present study we sought to fully evaluate a range of cognitive abilities (i.e., working memory, attention control, episodic and semantic memory, and fluid and crystallized intelligence) previously associated with multiply-constrained problem solving. Additionally, we sought to determine whether problem solving ability and strategies (analytical or insightful) were task specific or domain general through the use of novel problem solving tasks (TriBond and Location Bond). Multiply-constrained problem solving abilities were shown to be domain general, solutions derived through insightful strategies were more often correct than those derived through analytical strategies, and crystallized intelligence was the only cognitive ability that provided unique predictive value after accounting for all other abilities.

papers.title: Heuristics and representational change in two-move matchstick tasks
papers.abstract: Insight problems are problems where the problem solver struggles to find a solution until * aha! * the solution suddenly appears. Two contemporary theories suggest that insight problems are difficult either because problem solvers begin with an incorrect representation of the problem, or that problem solvers apply inappropriate heuristics to the problem. The relative contributions of representational change and inappropriate heuristics on the process of insight problem solving was studied with a task that required the problem solver to move two matchsticks in order to transform an incorrect arithmetic statement into a correct one. Problem solvers (N = 120) worked on two different types of two-move matchstick arithmetic problems that both varied with respect to the effectiveness of heuristics and to the degree of a necessary representational change of the problem representation. A strong influence of representational change on solution rates was found whereas the influence of heuristics had minimal effects on solution rates. That is, the difficulty of insight problems within the two-move matchstick arithmetic domain is governed by the degree of representational change required. A model is presented that details representational change as the necessary condition for ensuring that appropriate heuristics can be applied on the proper problem representation.

papers.title: The Impact of Reasoning Step Length on Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Chain of Thought (CoT) is significant in improving the reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). However, the correlation between the effectiveness of CoT and the length of reasoning steps in prompts remains largely unknown. To shed light on this, we have conducted several empirical experiments to explore the relations. Specifically, we design experiments that expand and compress the rationale reasoning steps within CoT demonstrations while keeping all other factors constant. We have the following key findings. First, the results indicate that lengthening the reasoning steps in prompts, even without adding new information into the prompt, considerably enhances LLMs' reasoning abilities across multiple datasets. Alternatively, shortening the reasoning steps, even while preserving the key information, significantly diminishes the reasoning abilities of models. This finding highlights the importance of the number of steps in CoT prompts and provides practical guidance to make better use of LLMs' potential in complex problem-solving scenarios. Second, we also investigated the relationship between the performance of CoT and the rationales used in demonstrations. Surprisingly, the result shows that even incorrect rationales can yield favorable outcomes if they maintain the requisite length of inference. Third, we observed that the advantages of increasing reasoning steps are task-dependent: simpler tasks require fewer steps, whereas complex tasks gain significantly from longer inference sequences. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/The-Impact-of-Reasoning-Step-Length-on-Large-Language-Models

papers.title: The cost of thinking is similar between large reasoning models and humans
papers.abstract: Do neural network models capture the cognitive demands of human reasoning? Across seven reasoning tasks, we show that the length of the chain-of-thought generated by large reasoning models predicts human reaction times both within tasks-tracking item-level difficulty-and across tasks-capturing broader differences in cognitive demands. This model-to-human alignment shows that out-of-the-box reasoning models reflect core features underlying problem and task complexity in human cognition, without requiring any built-in symbolic mechanisms.

papers.title: Mental Models or Probabilistic Reasoning or Both
papers.abstract: The present paper presents an overview of contemporary reasoning research to examine the evidence for and implications of the Dual Strategy Model of Reasoning. The Dual Strategy Model of Reasoning proposes that there are two types of reasoning strategy applied in deductive reasoning - counterexample and statistical. The paper considers Mental Models Theory and The Probability Heuristics Model as candidate specifications for these respective strategies and hypotheses are proposed on this basis. The Dual Strategy Model is further considered in the context of Dual Process theory, the Dual Source Model and Meta-reasoning and implications of the synergy between these proposals are considered. We finally consider the Dual Strategy Model in the context of individual differences, and normative considerations before proposing novel hypotheses and further avenues of research which we argue require exploration in this context.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Thought Anchors: Which LLM Reasoning Steps Matter?
papers.research_question: Which reasoning steps (sentences) in a chain-of-thought are important for guiding the reasoning trajectory and final answer?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sentence-level analysis methods (black-box resampling and white-box attention analysis) to identify 'thought anchors'—critical reasoning steps that guide the trajectory of chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Sentence-level analysis provides a promising intermediate abstraction for understanding reasoning in LLMs, with methods converging to identify critical 'thought anchor' steps that structure the reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
Plan generation and uncertainty management sentences have higher counterfactual importance than active computation or fact retrieval sentences.
Specialized 'receiver' attention heads consistently attend to thought anchor sentences, providing a mechanistic correlate of importance.
Sentence-sentence causal graphs reveal that stronger close-range links and weaker long-range links correlate with higher reasoning accuracy, especially in mathematical domains.
papers.limitation: The counterfactual importance metric can yield high-variance estimates when the number of semantically divergent resampled sentences is low.
future_direction: Investigating adaptive scales for defining reasoning steps beyond fixed sentences.
Further work on the limitations of the counterfactual importance metric with limited data.
papers.abstract: Current frontier large-language models rely on reasoning to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Many existing interpretability are limited in this area, as standard methods have been designed to study single forward passes of a model rather than the multi-token computational steps that unfold during reasoning. We argue that analyzing reasoning traces at the sentence level is a promising approach to understanding reasoning processes. We introduce a black-box method that measures each sentence's counterfactual importance by repeatedly sampling replacement sentences from the model, filtering for semantically different ones, and continuing the chain of thought from that point onwards to quantify the sentence's impact on the distribution of final answers. We discover that certain sentences can have an outsized impact on the trajectory of the reasoning trace and final answer. We term these sentences \textit{thought anchors}. These are generally planning or uncertainty management sentences, and specialized attention heads consistently attend from subsequent sentences to thought anchors. We further show that examining sentence-sentence causal links within a reasoning trace gives insight into a model's behavior. Such information can be used to predict a problem's difficulty and the extent different question domains involve sequential or diffuse reasoning. As a proof-of-concept, we demonstrate that our techniques together provide a practical toolkit for analyzing reasoning models by conducting a detailed case study of how the model solves a difficult math problem, finding that our techniques yield a consistent picture of the reasoning trace's structure. We provide an open-source tool (thought-anchors.com) for visualizing the outputs of our methods on further problems. The convergence across our methods shows the potential of sentence-level analysis for a deeper understanding of reasoning models.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Understanding Reasoning in Chain-of-Thought from the Hopfieldian View
papers.research_question: How does the reasoning capability emerge through Chain-of-Thought prompting? The paper aims to explain the fundamental factors behind CoT's success.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a Hopfieldian view of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, connecting it to cognitive neuroscience, and proposes the Representation-of-Thought framework to enhance robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a Hopfieldian framework for CoT interpretability, introducing error localization and the RoT framework, which improves robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
The Hopfieldian view provides a framework to understand CoT reasoning as movement between representation spaces.
A method for localizing reasoning errors in CoT responses is developed based on low-dimensional representation spaces.
The Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework enhances the robustness of CoT reasoning by manipulating hidden states towards representation spaces.
Experimental results show RoT improves accuracy on arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.
RoT offers fine-grained control over the reasoning process and improves interpretability.
future_direction: Exploring other elements of the Hopfieldian view such as attractors and state space.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have demonstrated remarkable abilities across various tasks, with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting emerging as a key technique to enhance reasoning capabilities. However, existing research primarily focuses on improving performance, lacking a comprehensive framework to explain and understand the fundamental factors behind CoT's success. To bridge this gap, we introduce a novel perspective grounded in the Hopfieldian view of cognition in cognitive neuroscience. We establish a connection between CoT reasoning and key cognitive elements such as stimuli, actions, neural populations, and representation spaces. From our view, we can understand the reasoning process as the movement between these representation spaces. Building on this insight, we develop a method for localizing reasoning errors in the response of CoTs. Moreover, we propose the Representation-of-Thought (RoT) framework, which leverages the robustness of low-dimensional representation spaces to enhance the robustness of the reasoning process in CoTs. Experimental results demonstrate that RoT improves the robustness and interpretability of CoT reasoning while offering fine-grained control over the reasoning process.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Understanding Hidden Computations in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do transformer models internally process and represent reasoning steps when Chain-of-Thought is replaced with filler characters, and can these hidden characters be recovered?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that hidden characters in filler Chain-of-Thought sequences can be recovered by analyzing layer-wise representations and token rankings without loss of performance, providing insights into internal mechanisms of transformer models.
papers.conclusion: The analysis sheds light on how models internally process and represent reasoning steps when explicit chain of thought is obscured, contributing to model interpretability and opening avenues for improving transparency in language model reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Layer-wise analysis reveals that filler tokens emerge in later layers, overwriting earlier numerical representations.
Token ranking analysis shows that original reasoning tokens remain among lower-ranked candidates beneath filler tokens.
A modified decoding algorithm can recover hidden characters by selecting non-filler tokens when fillers are top-ranked, without compromising task performance.
The model performs necessary computations in earlier layers and then overwrites intermediate representations with filler tokens in later layers to match training targets.
The findings suggest that models retain hidden reasoning steps internally even when outputting filler tokens.
papers.limitation: Focuses on a synthetic task (3SUM) and a relatively small transformer model, which may not capture complexities of real-world language tasks and larger models.
future_direction: Explore whether specific circuits, such as induction heads or particular attention patterns, are involved in overwriting behavior.
Apply similar analysis techniques to other tasks and models to assess the generality of the findings.
Extend the investigation to natural language tasks and larger models to determine if observed phenomena persist in more complex settings.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning abilities of large language models. However, recent studies have shown that models can still perform complex reasoning tasks even when the CoT is replaced with filler(hidden) characters (e.g., "..."), leaving open questions about how models internally process and represent reasoning steps. In this paper, we investigate methods to decode these hidden characters in transformer models trained with filler CoT sequences. By analyzing layer-wise representations using the logit lens method and examining token rankings, we demonstrate that the hidden characters can be recovered without loss of performance. Our findings provide insights into the internal mechanisms of transformer models and open avenues for improving interpretability and transparency in language model reasoning.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: From Sparse Dependence to Sparse Attention: Unveiling How Chain-of-Thought Enhances Transformer Sample Efficiency
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) improve the sample efficiency of transformers in learning parity functions, and does it do so by introducing sparse sequential dependencies that lead to sparse attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: CoT improves sample efficiency by introducing sparse sequential dependencies in the data, which transformers learn to capture with sparse and interpretable attention patterns, enabling polynomial sample complexity instead of exponential.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought enhances transformer sample efficiency by creating sparse sequential dependencies that are efficiently captured through sparse attention patterns, leading to polynomial sample complexity for learning parity functions.
papers.key_findings:
Without CoT, learning parity functions requires exponentially many samples in the hardness parameter k, while with CoT, it requires only polynomial samples.
CoT introduces sparse sequential dependencies among input tokens, which transformers learn to represent with sparse attention patterns.
The sparsity of attention layers, measured by normalized attention entropy, is crucial for the sample efficiency improvement induced by CoT.
Multi-pass training without CoT can also lead to sparse attention and learning, but is significantly less efficient than training with CoT.
Real-world CoT data (GSM8K) induces sparser attention patterns in pretrained language models compared to non-CoT data.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to more complex tasks and architectures
Exploring how sparsity can be leveraged to design more efficient training methods
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) significantly enhances the reasoning performance of large language models (LLM). While current theoretical studies often attribute this improvement to increased expressiveness and computational capacity, we argue that expressiveness is not the primary limitation in the LLM regime, as current large models will fail on simple tasks. Using a parity-learning setup, we demonstrate that CoT can substantially improve sample efficiency even when the representation power is sufficient. Specifically, with CoT, a transformer can learn the function within polynomial samples, whereas without CoT, the required sample size is exponential. Additionally, we show that CoT simplifies the learning process by introducing sparse sequential dependencies among input tokens, and leads to a sparse and interpretable attention. We validate our theoretical analysis with both synthetic and real-world experiments, confirming that sparsity in attention layers is a key factor of the improvement induced by CoT.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: When More is Less: Understanding Chain-of-Thought Length in LLMs
papers.research_question: Does reasoning performance consistently improve as Chain-of-Thought (CoT) processes grow longer, and what is the optimal CoT length?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that an optimal Chain-of-Thought length exists, following an inverted U-shaped curve with performance, and that this optimal length scales with task difficulty and model capability, revealing a simplicity bias where more capable models prefer shorter CoTs.
papers.conclusion: CoT length should be calibrated adaptively based on task complexity and model capability to optimize reasoning performance, moving beyond the assumption that longer is always better.
papers.key_findings:
Task accuracy versus CoT length follows an inverted U-shaped curve, indicating an optimal length.
The optimal CoT length increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability (simplicity bias).
Reinforcement learning training guides models towards generating CoTs of optimal length.
Training models on data with optimal-length CoTs improves their reasoning performance.
Filtering out excessively long CoTs at inference using a length-aware voting method improves accuracy.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) employ Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning to deconstruct complex problems. While longer CoTs are often presumed superior, this paper challenges that notion, arguing that longer is not always better. Drawing on combined evidence from real-world observations, controlled experiments, and theoretical analysis, we demonstrate that task accuracy typically follows an inverted U-shaped curve with CoT length, where performance initially improves but eventually decreases as the number of CoT steps increases. With controlled experiments, we further uncover the scaling behaviors of the optimal CoT length: it increases with task difficulty but decreases with model capability, exposing an inherent simplicity bias where more capable models favor shorter, more efficient CoT reasoning. This bias is also evident in Reinforcement Learning (RL) training, where models gravitate towards shorter CoTs as their accuracy improves. To have a deep understanding of these dynamics, we establish a simple theoretical model that formally proves these phenomena, including the optimal length's scaling laws and the emergence of simplicity bias during RL. Guided by this framework, we demonstrate significant practical benefits from training with optimally-lengthed CoTs and employing length-aware filtering at inference. These findings offer both a principled understanding of the "overthinking" phenomenon and multiple practical guidelines for CoT calibration, enabling LLMs to achieve optimal reasoning performance with adaptive CoTs tailored to task complexity and model capability.

papers.title: Reasoning as State Transition: A Representational Analysis of Reasoning Evolution in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How does reasoning ability evolve during training in large language models, and what is the role of internal representation dynamics in this process?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a representational analysis framework showing that post-training yields limited improvement in static initial representation quality, but reasoning involves a continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, which post-training enhances to drive representations toward a better state for task solving.
papers.conclusion: The work provides a novel representational perspective on reasoning evolution in LLMs, highlighting the importance of internal state dynamics and the role of post-training in enhancing state transitions, offering insights for future model analysis and optimization.
papers.key_findings:
Post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality.
Reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation, unlike non-reasoning tasks.
Post-training empowers models to drive this representation transition toward a better distribution for task solving.
There is a high correlation between generation correctness and final representations, but low correlation with initial representations.
The semantic content of the generated tokens is the dominant driver of the state transition, not additional computation or intrinsic parameter differences.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models have achieved remarkable performance on reasoning tasks, motivating research into how this ability evolves during training. Prior work has primarily analyzed this evolution via explicit generation outcomes, treating the reasoning process as a black box and obscuring internal changes. To address this opacity, we introduce a representational perspective to investigate the dynamics of the model's internal states. Through comprehensive experiments across models at various training stages, we discover that post-training yields only limited improvement in static initial representation quality. Furthermore, we reveal that, distinct from non-reasoning tasks, reasoning involves a significant continuous distributional shift in representations during generation. Comparative analysis indicates that post-training empowers models to drive this transition toward a better distribution for task solving. To clarify the relationship between internal states and external outputs, statistical analysis confirms a high correlation between generation correctness and the final representations; while counterfactual experiments identify the semantics of the generated tokens, rather than additional computation during inference or intrinsic parameter differences, as the dominant driver of the transition. Collectively, we offer a novel understanding of the reasoning process and the effect of training on reasoning enhancement, providing valuable insights for future model analysis and optimization.

papers.title: Unveiling Confirmation Bias in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does confirmation bias affect chain-of-thought reasoning behavior in LLMs, and why does its influence vary across questions, reasoning types, and models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that confirmation bias is pervasive in LLMs' chain-of-thought reasoning, affecting both reasoning generation and answer prediction, and explains variance in CoT effectiveness across tasks and models.
papers.conclusion: The study shows that confirmation bias significantly impacts CoT reasoning in LLMs, explaining performance variance across tasks and models, and highlights the difficulty of debiasing strong beliefs.
papers.key_findings:
Internal beliefs (approximated by direct QA probabilities) significantly influence CoT performance at both reasoning generation and answer prediction stages.
Questions with stronger beliefs (lower entropy) are more likely to retain correctness regardless of difficulty, showing confirmation bias.
CoT improvement aligns with the degree to which tasks are prone to confirmation bias, with greater improvement on symbolic reasoning (e.g., math) than on non-symbolic tasks.
Models with weaker beliefs (higher entropy) are more sensitive to the quality and structure of the generated rationale.
Debiasing internal beliefs is challenging, especially when beliefs are strong, as models struggle to follow rationales that contradict their confident prior beliefs.
papers.limitation: The use of entropy as a proxy for belief strength limits analysis to white-box LLMs and multiple-choice questions.
future_direction: Explore confirmation bias using confidence measures applicable to black-box LLMs and open-ended questions.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting has been widely adopted to enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs).However, the effectiveness of CoT reasoning is inconsistent across tasks with different reasoning types.This work presents a novel perspective to understand CoT behavior through the lens of confirmation bias in cognitive psychology.Specifically, we examine how model internal beliefs, approximated by direct questionanswering probabilities, affect both reasoning generation (Q R) and reasoning-guided answer prediction (QR A) in CoT.By decomposing CoT into a two-stage process, we conduct a thorough correlation analysis in model beliefs, rationale attributes, and stage-wise performance.Our results provide strong evidence of confirmation bias in LLMs, such that model beliefs not only skew the reasoning process but also influence how rationales are utilized for answer prediction.Furthermore, the interplay between task vulnerability to confirmation bias and the strength of beliefs also provides explanations for CoT effectiveness across reasoning tasks and models.Overall, this study provides a valuable insight for the needs of better prompting strategies that mitigate confirmation bias to enhance reasoning performance.Code is available at https://github.com/yuewan2/biasedcot.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: Iteration Head: A Mechanistic Study of Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: How does Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning emerge in transformers, and what are the inner workings and conditions for its appearance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers through the identification and analysis of a specialized attention mechanism called an 'iteration head', which enables efficient iterative reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn to solve iterative tasks efficiently via CoT reasoning by developing inner circuits (iteration heads) dedicated to multistep reasoning, and data curation can guide this process.
papers.key_findings:
Iteration heads, a specific pattern of weights in the first two attention layers, emerge in transformers trained on iterative tasks with CoT.
These heads enable the transformer to solve iterative tasks efficiently by retrieving the current input and previous state to compute the next state.
The iterative reasoning skill granted by iteration heads is transferable between different iterative tasks (e.g., from copying to parity).
Data curation (including easier tasks in training) can guide the model towards learning the iteration head circuit.
Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a limitation for complex iterative algorithms.
papers.limitation: Transformers are stateless models, requiring generated states to have a token representation for CoT, which is a shortcoming for complex iterative algorithms or generic language modeling.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning is known to improve Large Language Models both empirically and in terms of theoretical approximation power. However, our understanding of the inner workings and conditions of apparition of CoT capabilities remains limited. This paper helps fill this gap by demonstrating how CoT reasoning emerges in transformers in a controlled and interpretable setting. In particular, we observe the appearance of a specialized attention mechanism dedicated to iterative reasoning, which we coined "iteration heads". We track both the emergence and the precise working of these iteration heads down to the attention level, and measure the transferability of the CoT skills to which they give rise between tasks.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought in Large Language Models: Decoding, Projection, and Activation
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting in large language models? Specifically, does the model merely mimic exemplars, what changes occur in the projection space (logits), and does CoT enable deeper and broader utilization of pre-trained knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: This work analyzes the internal mechanisms of Chain-of-Thought prompting, finding that LLMs imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with question understanding, exhibit fluctuating but ultimately more concentrated logits distributions, and activate a broader set of neurons in final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought prompting enhances LLM reasoning by guiding models to imitate exemplar formats, focus logits distributions, and activate a broader set of knowledge-related neurons, leading to more accurate and confident answers.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs imitate the format of CoT exemplars (e.g., using sequence words like 'first', 'then') while generating personalized responses based on their understanding of the question.
During CoT generation, token logits fluctuate more than with standard prompts, but the final answer generation shows a more concentrated logits distribution, suggesting clearer direction.
CoT prompts lead to a broader range and higher intensity of neuron activations in the final layers compared to standard prompts, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval from pre-training.
Successful imitation of transferred CoT prompts correlates with higher answer accuracy, suggesting that understanding the exemplar format is key to CoT's effectiveness.
The probability distribution over candidate answers at the answer generation step is more concentrated (lower entropy) under CoT prompting, indicating higher model confidence in the selected answer.
papers.limitation: Experiments were conducted on a limited sample of 50 test examples per dataset due to budget constraints.
future_direction: Extend the analysis to more models and tasks.
Explore the dynamic changes in neuron activations across different layers.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought prompting has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models, with numerous studies exploring factors influencing its performance. However, the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. To further demystify the operational principles, this work examines three key aspects: decoding, projection, and activation, aiming to elucidate the changes that occur within models when employing Chainof-Thought. Our findings reveal that LLMs effectively imitate exemplar formats while integrating them with their understanding of the question, exhibiting fluctuations in token logits during generation but ultimately producing a more concentrated logits distribution, and activating a broader set of neurons in the final layers, indicating more extensive knowledge retrieval compared to standard prompts. Our code and data will be publicly avialable when the paper is accepted.

papers.title: Scaling Competence, Shrinking Reasoning: Cognitive Signatures in Language Model Learning
papers.research_question: How do reasoning tokens evolve during fine-tuning, and can they serve as indicators of learning stages?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning tokens in language models expand, peak, and contract during fine-tuning, mirroring the Four Stages of Competence, and their dynamics can serve as metrics for diagnosing training stages and guiding early stopping.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens serve as a dynamic scaffold during fine-tuning, providing insights into model learning dynamics and practical tools for diagnosing training progress and optimizing learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning token length increases with performance early in training, peaks at conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task.
Models retain task performance after training even when reasoning tokens are removed, indicating that reasoning scaffolds learning but becomes unnecessary once competence is acquired.
The progression of reasoning tokens aligns with the Four Stages of Competence framework from cognitive science.
Reasoning token dynamics can diagnose training stages, detect convergence, and inform early stopping criteria.
The pattern is consistent across multiple models and tasks including code generation, math problems, and logical question answering.
papers.limitation:
Reasoning token length and correctness are surface-level proxies for internal cognitive processes, and the use of competence stages is interpretive rather than diagnostic.
Experiments are limited to math, logic, and code generation tasks, and may not generalize to tasks with high ambiguity or contextual sensitivity.
The proposed metrics may be less stable in settings with noisy supervision, curriculum learning, or large-scale instruction tuning.
future_direction: Future work may formalize these analogies further or challenge them with deeper mechanistic analysis.
papers.abstract: We analyze reasoning in language models during task-specific fine-tuning and draws parallel between reasoning tokens--intermediate steps generated while solving problem and the human working memory. Drawing from cognitive science, we align training dynamics with the Four Stages of Competence: models initially produce incorrect outputs without reasoning, then begin reasoning (but still fail), eventually reason effectively, and finally solve tasks without explicit reasoning. We find that reasoning token length expands as performance improves, peaks at the stage of conscious competence, then declines as the model internalizes the task. Notably, after training, models retain performance even when reasoning is removed--suggesting it scaffolded learning but is no longer needed. This progression offers actionable insights: reasoning token dynamics can serve as a signal for diagnosing training stage, identifying convergence, and guiding early stopping. We propose metrics to track this trajectory and argue that reasoning behavior is valuable for understanding and optimizing reasoning model training.

papers.title: Don't Take Things Out of Context: Attention Intervention for Enhancing Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism by which isolated tokens in few-shot Chain-of-Thought demonstrations disrupt reasoning in LLMs, and how can we intervene to suppress this effect?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Few-shot Attention Intervention (FAI), a method that dynamically analyzes attention patterns to identify and suppress the distracting effect of isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations, thereby enhancing reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: FAI effectively recalibrates attention allocation to prevent LLMs from fixating on isolated tokens, enhancing reasoning performance across benchmarks.
papers.key_findings:
Isolated tokens in CoT demonstrations can disrupt reasoning by causing the model to take information out of context.
Tokens with specific attention characteristics (high self-attention, direct influence on output) are responsible for this distracting effect.
FAI effectively identifies such tokens and improves performance across multiple reasoning benchmarks.
FAI improves accuracy on AQuA by 5.91% and on other datasets.
The distracting effect is estimated to cause about 60% of errors in certain cases.
papers.limitation: Experiments are confined to LLMs with parameter scale between 7 billion and 13 billion due to hardware constraints.
future_direction: Investigating larger models to gain further insights.
papers.abstract: Few-shot Chain-of-Thought (CoT) significantly enhances the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), functioning as a whole to guide these models in generating reasoning steps toward final answers. However, we observe that isolated segments, words, or tokens within CoT demonstrations can unexpectedly disrupt the generation process of LLMs. The model may overly concentrate on certain local information present in the demonstration, introducing irrelevant noise into the reasoning process and potentially leading to incorrect answers. In this paper, we investigate the underlying mechanism of CoT through dynamically tracing and manipulating the inner workings of LLMs at each output step, which demonstrates that tokens exhibiting specific attention characteristics are more likely to induce the model to take things out of context; these tokens directly attend to the hidden states tied with prediction, without substantial integration of non-local information. Building upon these insights, we propose a Few-shot Attention Intervention method (FAI) that dynamically analyzes the attention patterns of demonstrations to accurately identify these tokens and subsequently make targeted adjustments to the attention weights to effectively suppress their distracting effect on LLMs. Comprehensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over baseline methods, with a remarkable 5.91% improvement on the AQuA dataset, further highlighting the effectiveness of FAI.

papers.title: Towards Understanding Chain-of-Thought Prompting: An Empirical Study of What Matters
papers.research_question: What makes Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance? Specifically, are ground truth bridging objects/language templates important, and if not, what are the key aspects needed for the LLM to reason properly?
papers.core_contribution: The validity of reasoning in Chain-of-Thought demonstrations is not crucial for performance; instead, the relevance of the rationale to the query and the coherence (correct ordering) of the reasoning steps are the key aspects that determine the effectiveness of CoT prompting.
papers.conclusion: The study deepens understanding of CoT prompting by showing that valid reasoning in demonstrations is not the primary driver of performance; instead, relevance and coherence are critical. This suggests LLMs' reasoning abilities largely come from pretraining, and CoT demonstrations mainly regularize the output format.
papers.key_findings:
Providing demonstrations with completely invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance of standard CoT prompting, indicating that logical validity in the examples is not essential.
Relevance (the rationale being based on the query) and coherence (the correct ordering of steps) are identified as the two key aspects for effective CoT prompting.
Relevance is more important than coherence for bridging objects (e.g., numbers, entities), while coherence of language templates is particularly important.
When both relevance and coherence are removed, performance drops significantly, sometimes below standard prompting without rationales.
The findings suggest LLMs may not be learning to reason from the demonstrations but rather using pretrained abilities, with CoT mainly specifying an output format that regularizes generation to be step-by-step, in order, and relevant.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are limited to two types of reasoning tasks (arithmetic reasoning and multi-hop question answering); other tasks like symbolic reasoning were not studied due to their highly template-based nature.
The construction of invalid reasoning demonstrations was done manually, lacking a systematic treatment; automatically synthesizing such rationales is challenging.
Intrinsic evaluation relies on the correctness of bridging objects, which may not be a comprehensive metric and requires costly annotation.
future_direction: Extending the ablation designs to other types of reasoning tasks, such as symbolic reasoning tasks where steps have little variation.
Developing a more systematic treatment of the 'invalid reasoning' setting, e.g., by categorizing informal logical fallacies.
Improving intrinsic evaluation methods to be more comprehensive and reference-free.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting can dramatically improve the multi-step reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs). CoT explicitly encourages the LLM to generate intermediate rationales for solving a problem, by providing a series of reasoning steps in the demonstrations. Despite its success, there is still little understanding of what makes CoT prompting effective and which aspects of the demonstrated reasoning steps contribute to its performance. In this paper, we show that CoT reasoning is possible even with invalid demonstrations - prompting with invalid reasoning steps can achieve over 80-90% of the performance obtained using CoT under various metrics, while still generating coherent lines of reasoning during inference. Further experiments show that other aspects of the rationales, such as being relevant to the query and correctly ordering the reasoning steps, are much more important for effective CoT reasoning. Overall, these findings both deepen our understanding of CoT prompting, and open up new questions regarding LLMs' capability to learn to reason in context.

papers.title: Distributional reasoning in LLMs: Parallel reasoning processes in multi-hop reasoning
papers.research_question: What strategy does an LLM use to solve multi-hop reasoning questions when not explicitly writing down a thought process (i.e., without chain-of-thought)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that during multi-hop reasoning, LLMs internally activate a distribution of potential intermediate answers in middle layers, and the final answer can be approximated via a linear transformation from this distribution, revealing parallel reasoning paths.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ a distributional reasoning process for multi-hop questions, characterized by parallel activation of intermediate possibilities and a linear transformation to final answers, bridging associative and propositional reasoning approaches.
papers.key_findings:
The activation vector of potential final answers (A2) can be linearly approximated from the activation vector of potential intermediate answers (A1) extracted from middle layers, with R^2 > 0.5 on average.
Middle layers generate highly interpretable embeddings representing a set of potential intermediate answers, followed by a phase transition where A1 activations decrease and A2 activations increase.
High Spearman correlation exists between the order of top-activated A1 logits in middle layers and their corresponding A2 logits in the output layer.
The same distributional reasoning process occurs even when the model hallucinates answers (on fictitious subjects or out-of-distribution attributes).
The reasoning process is largely handled at the final token position after the middle layers, with minimal influence from other token positions.
papers.limitation:
The questions have a similar general structure; altering the structure could lead to different results.
Different prompt structures, question types, or subjects could lead the model to employ various solving strategies.
The analysis cannot account for semantic categories that lack clear representative tokens (e.g., years).
The statistical analyses do not show direct causality.
future_direction: Explore mechanisms for semantic categories lacking clear representative tokens.
Investigate direct causality in the observed process.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown an impressive ability to perform tasks believed to require thought processes. When the model does not document an explicit thought process, it becomes difficult to understand the processes occurring within its hidden layers and to determine if these processes can be referred to as reasoning. We introduce a novel and interpretable analysis of internal multi-hop reasoning processes in LLMs. We demonstrate that the prediction process for compositional reasoning questions can be modeled using a simple linear transformation between two semantic category spaces. We show that during inference, the middle layers of the network generate highly interpretable embeddings that represent a set of potential intermediate answers for the multi-hop question. We use statistical analyses to show that a corresponding subset of tokens is activated in the model's output, implying the existence of parallel reasoning paths. These observations hold true even when the model lacks the necessary knowledge to solve the task. Our findings can help uncover the strategies that LLMs use to solve reasoning tasks, offering insights into the types of thought processes that can emerge from artificial intelligence. Finally, we also discuss the implication of cognitive modeling of these results.

papers.title: Why think step by step? Reasoning emerges from the locality of experience
papers.research_question: Why is chain-of-thought reasoning useful in language models? The paper tests the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that chain-of-thought reasoning is effective when training data has local structure, allowing models to chain accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables not seen together in training.
papers.conclusion: The effectiveness of chain-of-thought reasoning in language models is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias in conditional probability estimation when training data is locally structured.
Free generation, where the model chooses intermediate variables, performs similarly to scaffolded generation with ideal intermediates.
Reasoning does not help when training data is fully observed or has the wrong locality structure.
The combination of locally structured training data and reasoning is more data-efficient than training on fully observed data.
When models fail to estimate conditional probabilities accurately, their estimates tend to match marginal probabilities.
papers.limitation: The study uses a simplified synthetic setting, which may not fully capture natural language data.
papers.abstract: Humans have a powerful and mysterious capacity to reason. Working through a set of mental steps enables us to make inferences we would not be capable of making directly even though we get no additional data from the world. Similarly, when large language models generate intermediate steps (a chain of thought) before answering a question, they often produce better answers than they would directly. We investigate why and how chain-of-thought reasoning is useful in language models, testing the hypothesis that reasoning is effective when training data consists of overlapping local clusters of variables that influence each other strongly. These training conditions enable the chaining of accurate local inferences to estimate relationships between variables that were not seen together in training. We prove that there will exist a "reasoning gap", where reasoning through intermediate variables reduces bias, for the simple case of an autoregressive density estimator trained on local samples from a chain-structured probabilistic model. We then test our hypothesis experimentally in more complex models, training an autoregressive language model on samples from Bayes nets but only including a subset of variables in each sample. We test language models' ability to match conditional probabilities with and without intermediate reasoning steps, finding that intermediate steps are only helpful when the training data is locally structured with respect to dependencies between variables. The combination of locally structured observations and reasoning is much more data-efficient than training on all variables. Our results illustrate how the effectiveness of reasoning step by step is rooted in the local statistical structure of the training data.

papers.title: A Closer Look at Bias and Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness of Large (Vision) Language Models
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully reflect model internal processes in large vision-language models? How do text-based and image-based biases affect reasoning and bias articulation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for CoT faithfulness in LVLMs, finding that image-based biases are less articulated than text-based ones, and identifying inconsistent reasoning as a potential indicator of bias.
papers.conclusion: The study finds large variations in bias articulation rate depending on model training strategy and bias type, and identifies inconsistent reasoning as a failure mode. The 'reasonableness' of a bias affects articulation, and inconsistencies may signal biases in the absence of faithful CoTs.
papers.key_findings:
RL-trained reasoning models have substantially higher bias articulation rates compared to instruction-tuned or SFT-trained counterparts.
Visual biases are consistently less likely to be articulated than text-based biases, and subtle biases receive considerably less attention in model reasoning traces than explicit ones.
Models exhibit a previously unidentified phenomenon termed 'inconsistent reasoning' where they demonstrate correct reasoning before abruptly changing answers.
Inconsistent reasoning occurs more frequently when the bias conflicts with the ground truth, serving as a potential canary for detecting biased reasoning.
Bias articulation rates do not increase when given biased in-context samples, remaining constant across no-context, unbiased, and biased context settings.
papers.limitation:
They do not test faithfulness when inducing biases via training (as opposed to biased in-context samples).
They have yet to demonstrate detecting unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
They do not have a theory to explain why some biases are articulated at a higher rate than others.
future_direction: Exploring faithfulness when inducing biases via training.
Demonstrating detection of unfaithfulness when not explicit in the CoT in practical settings.
Developing a theory to explain differences in bias articulation rates.
